Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Scientists in Colombia have unearthed the remains of a true prehistoric monster believed to be the biggest snake ever to have lived on Earth. An artist's impression of what Titanoboa cerrejonensis would have looked like. Named Titanoboa cerrejonensis, the snake would have weighed 1,140 kilograms (2,500 pounds) and measured 13 meters (42.7 feet) nose to tail tip -- dwarfing the largest modern pythons and anacondas which can grow to 6 meters (19.5 feet). Scientists believe it slithered around the planet between 58 and 60 million years ago. Geologist David Polly, who identified the position of the fossil vertebrae which made a size estimate possible, said in a statement Wednesday: "At its greatest width, the snake would have come up to about your hips. The size is pretty amazing. "But our team went a step further and asked, how warm would the Earth have to be to support a body of this size?" Titanoboa's fossilized remains were discovered at a coal mine in the tropical Cerrejon region of northern Colombia by an international team of scientists. "Truly enormous snakes really spark people's imagination, but reality has exceeded the fantasies of Hollywood," paleontologist Jonathan Bloch, who co-led the expedition, told reporters. "The snake that tried to eat Jennifer Lopez in the movie 'Anaconda' was not as big as the one we found." Based on the snake's size, the team was able to calculate that the mean annual temperature in equatorial South America 60 million years ago would have been about 91 degrees Fahrenheit, about 10 degrees warmer than today, Bloch said. "Tropical ecosystems of South America were surprisingly different 60 million years ago," said Bloch. "It was a rainforest, like today, but it was even hotter and the cold-blooded reptiles were all substantially larger. "The result was, among other things, the largest snakes the world has ever seen...and hopefully ever will." According to Nature.com, snakes are poikilotherms (cold-blooded) that, unlike humans, need heat from their environment to power their metabolism. Therefore research suggests that at the time the region would have had to be no less than 86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit for the snake to have survived. Most large snakes today live in the tropical regions of South America and south-east Asia, where the high temperatures allow them to grow to impressive sizes. Meanwhile, Carlos Jaramillo -- who was also part of the expedition -- said the tropical rainforest at Cerrejon appeared to have thrived at these temperatures. "This data challenges the view that tropical vegetation lives near its climatic optimum, and it has profound implications in understanding the effect of current global warming on tropical plants," he said.

The snake is estimated to have weighed about 1,140 kilograms, or 2,500 pounds, and stretched roughly 13 meters, or 42.7 feet, from its snout to the end of its tail. That would make it far larger than today’s biggest pythons and anacondas, which can reach around 6 meters, or 19.5 feet, in length.

Scientists believe *Titanoboa* lived approximately 58 to 60 million years ago. David Polly, a geologist who determined the placement of the fossil vertebrae and helped make the size estimate possible, said in a statement Wednesday that the snake’s widest point would have reached about hip height on a person. “The size is pretty amazing,” he said. He added that the research team then took the question further by asking how warm Earth would have needed to be to sustain an animal of such enormous size.

The fossilized bones were found by an international group of scientists in a coal mine in the tropical Cerrejon area of northern Colombia.

Paleontologist Jonathan Bloch, who helped lead the expedition, said the discovery goes beyond anything imagined in films. He told reporters that giant snakes capture the public’s imagination, but in this case reality had surpassed Hollywood fantasy. He noted that the snake featured in the movie *Anaconda*, which attacked Jennifer Lopez’s character, was smaller than the fossil snake they discovered.

Using the animal’s size, the scientists calculated that the average yearly temperature in equatorial South America around 60 million years ago was about 91 degrees Fahrenheit — approximately 10 degrees warmer than it is today, Bloch said.

Bloch explained that tropical ecosystems in South America were very different at that time. Although the region was rainforest, as it is now, it was hotter, and cold-blooded reptiles grew much larger. One result, he said, was the existence of the largest snakes ever known — “and hopefully ever will” be known.

Nature.com notes that snakes are poikilotherms, or cold-blooded animals. Unlike humans, they depend on warmth from their surroundings to fuel their metabolism. Because of that, the research indicates that the region would have needed temperatures of at least 86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit for *Titanoboa* to survive.

Today, most very large snakes are found in tropical parts of South America and Southeast Asia, where consistently high temperatures help them reach great sizes.

Carlos Jaramillo, another member of the expedition, said evidence suggests that the tropical rainforest at Cerrejon flourished under those hot conditions. He said the findings challenge the idea that tropical plants already live close to their ideal climate limits, and that the data has important consequences for understanding how modern global warming may affect tropical vegetation.

# Giant Snake Fossils Reveal a Hotter Ancient Rainforest

Scientists studying fossils from Colombia made a discovery that sounded almost mythical: the remains of a prehistoric snake that stretched about 42 feet long and weighed more than a ton. Named *Titanoboa cerrejonensis*, the giant snake lived roughly 60 million years ago, not long after the extinction of the dinosaurs. Beyond revealing one of the largest snakes ever known, the fossils helped researchers estimate something surprising: the temperature of an ancient tropical rainforest.

The fossils were found in the Cerrejón coal mine in northern Colombia, a site that has preserved remains of one of the earliest known rainforests from the Paleocene epoch. Alongside the snake bones, scientists uncovered fossil plants, turtles, crocodile relatives, and fish, offering a detailed picture of a warm, wet ecosystem that existed millions of years before the rise of humans.

## Why a Snake Can Act Like a Thermometer

The key to the temperature estimate lies in snake biology. Snakes are ectotherms, often called “cold-blooded” animals, meaning they rely heavily on the surrounding environment to regulate their body temperature. Unlike mammals and birds, they do not generate enough internal heat to maintain a constant body temperature on their own.

Because of this, climate places limits on how large reptiles can grow. In general, larger ectotherms need consistently warm environments to keep their bodies functioning. If the climate is too cool, a giant snake would struggle to remain active, digest food, and survive.

By comparing *Titanoboa* with living snakes, especially large tropical species such as anacondas and pythons, scientists used the relationship between body size and environmental temperature to estimate the climate in which the animal lived.

## A Rainforest Warmer Than Today’s

Based on the enormous size of *Titanoboa*, researchers estimated that the rainforest where it lived had an average annual temperature of about 30 to 34 degrees Celsius, or roughly 86 to 93 degrees Fahrenheit. That is warmer than many modern tropical rainforests.

This was an important finding because the Paleocene was a time of high atmospheric carbon dioxide levels. The presence of such a large snake supported the idea that tropical ecosystems could become extremely warm under greenhouse conditions while still supporting lush forests and abundant wildlife.

The Cerrejón fossils showed that the region was not a dry desert despite the heat. Instead, it was a humid rainforest filled with rivers and swamps—an environment well suited to a massive predator like *Titanoboa*. Scientists believe the snake likely lived much like a modern anaconda, spending time in water and ambushing fish, crocodile-like reptiles, and other animals.

## A Window Into the Post-Dinosaur World

*Titanoboa* lived only a few million years after the asteroid impact that wiped out non-avian dinosaurs. Its discovery helped scientists understand how tropical ecosystems recovered and evolved after that mass extinction.

The fossils suggest that rainforests rebounded into rich, complex habitats relatively quickly in geological terms. Large reptiles occupied top predator roles, and warm temperatures allowed some species to reach extraordinary sizes.

## Scientific Debate and Caution

The temperature estimates based on *Titanoboa* have been influential, but they are not without debate. Some scientists have questioned whether body size in reptiles can be used as a precise thermometer, since factors such as food supply, habitat, evolution, and behavior also influence how large animals can become.

Still, the giant snake remains a powerful clue. When combined with fossil plants, ancient soils, and other geological evidence, *Titanoboa* helps build a broader picture of a hot, humid rainforest in northern South America around 60 million years ago.

## Why the Discovery Matters

The fossils of *Titanoboa* are more than evidence of an enormous prehistoric snake. They offer insight into how life responded to a warmer world. As modern climate change raises questions about the future of tropical ecosystems, ancient environments like Cerrejón provide valuable examples of how forests and animals once lived under much hotter conditions.

In that sense, the 42-foot snake from Colombia is not just a spectacular fossil. It is a climate clue from deep time—one that helps scientists understand both Earth’s past and its possible future.
